@fig-schema shows the flow. Two design choices deserve attention. First, **the burn-in stage had a specific statistical job**: equal randomization built the "prior probability of disease control for a given treatment in a given marker group" that the adaptive engine would consume afterwards [@kim2011]. The plan called for *at least* 80 equally randomized patients, sufficient — the designers judged — for every marker-group cell to contain at least one completed treatment [@kim2011]; in the event, equal randomization covered 97 patients (~38% of randomized patients), a point the team later flagged as a lesson (Section 6.2) [@kim2011; @liu2015]. Second, **eligibility restricted the adaptive engine**: arms had treatment-specific eligibility criteria, and only 14% of enrolled patients were eligible for all four arms, so the randomization denominator Ω shrank patient by patient [@liu2015].

## From 11 biomarkers to 5 marker groups

The biomarker panel was fixed in 2005 and prespecified before activation [@kim2011]. Tumors were tested for **mutations** of *EGFR*, *KRAS*, and *BRAF*; **copy number** (FISH) of *EGFR* and the cyclin D1 gene (*CCND1*); and **protein expression** (IHC) of VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα, RXRβ, RXRγ, and cyclin D1 — eleven markers in total [@kim2011]. Because dichotomizing eleven markers yields $2^{11} = 2{,}048$ possible profiles, the team collapsed them into **five ranked marker groups**, assigning each patient to the highest-ranked positive group (ranked by the strength of available 2005-era evidence), with a fifth group for patients negative for everything or with missing/incomplete data [@liu2015; @kim2011]:

| Rank | Marker group | Constituent biomarkers (any one positive) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | EGFR | *EGFR* mutation; *EGFR* amplification / high polysomy; increased *EGFR* copy number |
| 2 | KRAS/BRAF | *KRAS* mutation; *BRAF* mutation |
| 3 | VEGF/VEGFR-2 | VEGF overexpression; VEGFR-2 overexpression |
| 4 | RXR/cyclin D1 | RXRα, RXRβ, or RXRγ overexpression; cyclin D1 overexpression; *CCND1* amplification |
| 5 | None / unknown | No study biomarker positive, or biomarker data missing or incomplete |

: The five ranked marker groups. Grouping and ranking are documented in [@kim2011] (methods) and [@liu2015] (Table 1 description); the sequential "highest-ranked positive group wins" rule is explicit in both. {#tbl-markers}

Keep @tbl-markers in mind — the *grouping itself* became the trial's most-cited self-criticism (Sections 7 and 8): strong single-marker effects (e.g., *EGFR* mutation for erlotinib) were diluted when bundled with weaker markers in the same class [@kim2011; @liu2015].

## The Bayesian hierarchical probit model

BATTLE's outcome model is a **hierarchical probit model** — elegant, easy to Gibbs-sample, and pedagogically ideal because every piece has a trial-level meaning [@zhou2008]. For patient $i$ in arm $j \in \{1,2,3,4\}$ and marker group $k \in \{1,\dots,5\}$, define $y_{ijk} \in \{0,1\}$ as the 8-week disease-control indicator. Introduce a latent variable $z_{ijk}$:

$$
y_{ijk} = \mathbf{1}\{z_{ijk} > 0\}, \qquad z_{ijk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk},\, 1)
$$ {#eq-latent}

Here $\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}$ is the indicator function, $z_{ijk}$ is an unobserved "tolerance" that tips the patient into disease control when positive, and the variance is fixed at 1 for identifiability (the probit scale has no free scale parameter) [@zhou2008]. The disease-control probability for the cell $(j,k)$ is then a smooth function of the cell mean $\mu_{jk}$:

$$
\gamma_{jk} \;=\; \Pr(y_{ijk} = 1) \;=\; \Pr(z_{ijk} > 0) \;=\; \Phi(\mu_{jk}),
$$ {#eq-dcr}

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. Intuition: $\mu_{jk}$ is just the probit transform of the cell's DCR — e.g., a DCR of 0.46 corresponds to $\mu \approx 0.10$, and 0.58 to $\mu \approx 0.20$.

The hierarchy enters through the prior on the cell means. Within an arm, the five marker-group means are exchangeable around an arm-level effect $\phi_j$; the arm effects are themselves exchangeable around zero [@zhou2008]:

$$
\mu_{jk} \sim \mathcal{N}(\phi_j,\, \sigma^2) \quad (k = 1,\dots,5), \qquad
\phi_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, \tau^2) \quad (j = 1,\dots,4)
$$ {#eq-hier}

with $\sigma^2 = \tau^2 = 10^6$ as the default *vague* configuration [@zhou2008]. Read @eq-hier as two dials of **partial pooling**: small $\sigma^2$ makes the marker groups within an arm share information heavily (each group's estimate is pulled toward the arm effect $\phi_j$); small $\tau^2$ makes the arms share information with each other. BATTLE ran these dials essentially open (vague priors), so borrowing happened only where the data themselves were concordant — the model "learns how much to borrow" from the observed pattern of subgroup results [@zhou2008; @berrybook2010].

Given the observed disease-control indicators, the posterior combines a probit likelihood with the normal priors:

$$
p(\mu, \phi \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\;
\prod_{j=1}^{4} \prod_{k=1}^{5} \prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}
\Phi(\mu_{jk})^{y_{ijk}} \left[1 - \Phi(\mu_{jk})\right]^{1 - y_{ijk}}
\;\times\;
\prod_{j,k} \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jk} \mid \phi_j, \sigma^2)
\;\times\;
\prod_{j} \mathcal{N}(\phi_j \mid 0, \tau^2)
$$ {#eq-posterior}

The symbols in @eq-posterior: $n_{jk}$ is the number of patients randomized to arm $j$ within marker group $k$; $\mu$ collects all twenty cell means and $\phi$ the four arm effects. The trial team computed these posteriors by Gibbs sampling from the full conditionals — a workload that was heavy for 2006 but is trivial today, and that BATTLE-1 automated in R behind a web service (Section 6) [@zhou2008; @liu2015].

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Interpretation — why a probit rather than a logit?
The probit link is not a substantive claim about biology; it is a **computational convenience**. With normal priors on $\mu_{jk}$, the full conditionals are (truncated) normals, so Gibbs sampling is exact and fast — no Metropolis–Hastings tuning in the middle of a live trial. A logistic model with the same hierarchy (used later for BATTLE-2, [@lee2010]) would deliver nearly identical inferences; the choice reflects 2006-era Bayesian computation practice, an excellent example of letting the computing environment shape — not distort — the statistics.
:::

@fig-shrinkage makes the "borrowing strength" idea concrete with a small simulation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Illustrative simulation — partial pooling in one arm. Eight marker-group-like subgroups (n = 8 each) are generated from a probit-scale hierarchy similar in spirit to @eq-hier (subgroup means centered at a DCR of 40%, subgroup SD 0.35 on the probit scale). Open circles: raw subgroup DCRs. Filled circles: posterior-mean-style shrunk estimates $(x + \\kappa\\,\\bar p)/(n + \\kappa)$ with $\\kappa = 10$, a Beta–Binomial stand-in for the trial's probit-scale pooling. Subgroups whose raw rate is extreme are pulled toward the arm average — this is the 'borrowing strength' that stabilized all 20 cells of BATTLE-1 with small $n_{jk}$."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
set.seed(7)
k_grp <- 8; n_per <- 8; kappa <- 10
mu_sim   <- rnorm(k_grp, qnorm(0.40), 0.35)
p_true   <- pnorm(mu_sim)
x_sim    <- rbinom(k_grp, n_per, p_true)
p_raw    <- x_sim / n_per
p_bar    <- sum(x_sim) / (k_grp * n_per)
p_shrunk <- (x_sim + kappa * p_bar) / (n_per + kappa)
shr <- data.frame(group = factor(1:k_grp), p_raw, p_shrunk)
ggplot(shr, aes(x = group, xend = group)) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = p_raw, yend = p_shrunk), colour = "grey60",
               linewidth = 0.6, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(y = p_raw), shape = 21, size = 2.6, fill = "white", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(aes(y = p_shrunk), size = 2.6, colour = pal[1]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Simulated marker-group cell (one arm)",
       y = "8-week DCR estimate",
       title = "Partial pooling: raw vs. shrunk subgroup estimates") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.6, y = 0.92, size = 2.9,
           label = "open = raw subgroup rate\nfilled = shrunk toward arm mean")

```
## The adaptive-randomization engine

Once every one of the 20 cells (4 arms × 5 groups) contained at least one patient with a known outcome, randomization switched from equal to **outcome-adaptive**. For the next patient in marker group $k$, the probability of assignment to arm $j$ was proportional to the *posterior mean* disease-control rate of that cell, with two safeguards [@zhou2008]:

$$
w_{jk} \;=\; \frac{\hat\gamma_{jk}}{\sum_{\omega \in \Omega}\hat\gamma_{\omega k}},
\qquad
\hat\gamma_{jk} = \max\!\big\{\, \mathbb{E}[\gamma_{jk} \mid \text{data}],\; 0.10 \,\big\}
$$ {#eq-ar}

In @eq-ar, $\hat\gamma_{jk}$ is the posterior mean DCR for arm $j$ in group $k$ (floored at 0.10 so no non-suspended arm ever becomes essentially unreachable — the trial's explicit minimum-allocation device [@zhou2008]), and $\Omega$ is the set of arms that are both **non-suspended for futility** and **eligible for that patient** (recall: only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms [@liu2015]). The published worked example [@zhou2008] makes the weights tangible: if the current posterior mean DCRs in a marker group were 0.6, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1, the assignment probabilities become 0.50, 0.25, 0.17, and 0.08.

Two remarks for the practicing statistician. First, this is **covariate-adjusted adaptive randomization**: the weights are computed *within marker group*, so the adaptation respects the stratification — the trial learns "which arm works best *for tumors like this one*" rather than a single global winner. Second, BATTLE-1's rule is the plainest member of the broader family of Bayesian adaptive-randomization rules popularized by Thall and Wathen, who add a **power smoothing** so that early, noisy estimates do not over-steer allocation [@thall2007]:

$$
w_j^{(m)} \;=\; \frac{\bar p_j^{\,q(m)}}{\sum_{\ell} \bar p_\ell^{\,q(m)}},
\qquad
q(m) \;=\; \frac{m/4 + 8}{m},
$$ {#eq-tw}

where $m$ indexes trial progress, $\bar p_j$ is the current probability that arm $j$ is (or performs) best, and $q(m) > 1$ early (dampening) falls below 1 later (sharpening). BATTLE-1 used the unsmoothed proportional form of @eq-ar; its successor BATTLE-2 instead **bounded** the randomization probabilities (0.2–0.8 in stage 1, 0.1–0.9 in stage 2) to prevent extreme allocations from either noise or premature certainty [@liu2015]. If you implement one of these designs today, the choice among {no smoothing, power smoothing, probability bounds} is exactly the kind of decision to justify by simulation. @fig-ar shows what the BATTLE-1-style engine does in silico when seeded with the trial's own marginal response rates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ar
#| fig-cap: "Illustrative simulation — how outcome-adaptive randomization behaves. A Beta–Bernoulli approximation of @eq-ar (not the trial's probit model) allocates 244 sequential patients among four arms with true 8-week DCRs set to BATTLE's observed marginal rates (erlotinib 34%, vandetanib 33%, erlotinib + bexarotene 50%, sorafenib 58%; @kim2011). Each point is the assignment probability at that patient; the 10% floor of @eq-ar and normalization over arms are applied. Weights drift toward the better arms as evidence accumulates; note they start near 0.25 (equal) and remain noisy because only the assigned arm's outcome updates. In the real trial, additionally, 8-week outcomes arrive with delay, so the engine ran on partially stale data."
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 5
set.seed(41)
truth_ar <- c(E = 0.34, V = 0.33, EB = 0.50, S = 0.58)
n_pat <- 244
s_ar <- n_ar <- rep(0, 4)
w_hist <- matrix(NA_real_, n_pat, 4)
for (i in seq_len(n_pat)) {
  phat   <- (s_ar + 1) / (n_ar + 2)      # Beta(1,1) posterior mean
  w_arms <- pmax(phat, 0.10)             # 10% floor
  w_arms <- w_arms / sum(w_arms)
  w_hist[i, ] <- w_arms
  j <- sample(4, 1, prob = w_arms)
  n_ar[j] <- n_ar[j] + 1
  s_ar[j] <- s_ar[j] + rbinom(1, 1, truth_ar[j])
}
colnames(w_hist) <- names(truth_ar)
w_df <- as.data.frame(w_hist) |>
  mutate(patient = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-patient, names_to = "arm", values_to = "probability")
w_df$arm <- factor(w_df$arm, levels = names(truth_ar),
                   labels = c("erlotinib", "vandetanib",
                              "erlotinib + bexarotene", "sorafenib"))
ggplot(w_df, aes(patient, probability, colour = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Patient arrival (order)", y = "Assignment probability",
       title = "Simulated adaptive weights under BATTLE-like marginal DCRs") +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = 0.265, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40",
           label = "equal randomization (0.25)")

```

## Futility monitoring: suspension, not execution

After adaptive randomization began, each new outcome re-triggered a futility check for every cell. A cell was **suspended** — patients in marker group $k$ could no longer be randomized to arm $j$ — whenever

$$
\Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.50 \mid \text{data}\} \;\le\; 0.10,
$$ {#eq-futility}

i.e., when the data made it unlikely (posterior probability ≤ 10%) that the cell's true DCR exceeded the 50% target [@zhou2008; @liu2015]. Three features of this rule reward attention. **It is cell-specific**: the same arm could stay open for one marker group while suspended for another — the entire point of a biomarker-guided design. **It is reversible**: if later data (e.g., from other marker groups borrowed through the hierarchy) lifted the posterior back above the boundary, the cell reopened [@zhou2008]. And **there is no early stopping for efficacy**: success was only declared at trial end, so adaptation and inference could never race each other [@zhou2008]. The success rule itself, applied to every cell at the trial's close, was

$$
\Pr\{\gamma_{jk} > 0.30 \mid \text{data}\} \;\ge\; 0.80,
$$ {#eq-success}

i.e., a posterior probability of at least 0.80 that the cell's true DCR exceeds the 30% historical benchmark [@zhou2008; @kim2011].

```{r}
#| label: fig-futility
#| fig-cap: "Illustrative trajectory of the futility statistic in @eq-futility. For a cell whose observed DCR tracks a true rate of 30% (blue) the posterior probability Pr(DCR > 0.50 | data) decays quickly below the 0.10 suspension boundary; for a cell tracking 55% (green) it never approaches it. Computed analytically under a Beta(1,1) posterior with expected success counts $m p$ after $m$ evaluable patients (a deterministic stand-in for a single noisy path). In BATTLE-1 the same logic ran on actual outcomes for all 20 cells after every updated endpoint, with suspension reversible [@zhou2008]."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.8
m_seq <- 1:80
fut_curve <- function(p_true) {
  sapply(m_seq, function(mm) 1 - pbeta(0.50, mm * p_true + 1, mm * (1 - p_true) + 1))
}
fut_df <- data.frame(
  m = rep(m_seq, 2),
  prob = c(fut_curve(0.30), fut_curve(0.55)),
  scenario = rep(c("true DCR 30% (futile)", "true DCR 55% (active)"), each = length(m_seq)))
ggplot(fut_df, aes(m, prob, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.10, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], pal[3])) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number()) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.003, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Evaluable patients in the cell (arm × marker group)",
       y = "Pr(DCR > 0.50 | data)  [log scale]",
       title = "Cell-level futility statistic vs. the 0.10 suspension boundary") +
  annotate("text", x = 45, y = 0.115, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           label = "suspension boundary (0.10)")

```

# The biomarker engine: real-time tissue from relapsed lung cancer

## The pipeline, step by step

The boldest requirement of BATTLE was not statistical. Every enrolled patient had to consent to a **fresh tumor biopsy** after relapse — in a population already heavily treated, with lesions that are often hard to reach [@kim2011; @liu2015]. @fig-biopsyflow reconstructs the documented pipeline.

```{r}
#| label: fig-biopsyflow
#| fig-cap: "The real-time tissue pipeline (documented; diagram is didactic). An interventional radiologist obtained 1–3 fresh cores (~1 mm diameter, 1.2–1.8 cm long; minimum two cores required) under CT or ultrasound guidance; specimens were formalin-fixed immediately in the radiology suite; a molecular pathologist reviewed H&E sections within 24 hours (adequacy = at least 200 malignant cells); the 11-biomarker panel (mutations of EGFR/KRAS/BRAF; FISH copy number for EGFR and CCND1; IHC for VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα/β/γ, cyclin D1) was reported within two weeks; the marker group then fed the randomization engine. Sources: @kim2011 (methods), @liu2015."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.4
bx <- data.frame(
  x = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6),
  y = c(9.2, 7.35, 5.5, 3.65, 1.7),
  w = c(7.2, 6.6, 7.2, 8.2, 7.2),
  h = c(1.25, 1.0, 1.15, 1.55, 1.15),
  fill = c("#D9E8F5", "#DFF2E4", "#FDEBD0", "#E8E0F0", "#FBE3E0"),
  size = c(2.8, 2.75, 2.75, 2.6, 2.8),
  label = c(
    "Image-guided core-needle biopsy\n(1–3 fresh cores, ≥ 2 required)",
    "Formalin fixation immediately,\nin the interventional radiology suite",
    "Molecular pathologist H&E review within 24 h\n(adequate = ≥ 200 malignant cells)",
    "11-biomarker panel: mutations (EGFR, KRAS, BRAF);\nFISH (EGFR, CCND1); IHC (VEGF, VEGFR-2, RXRα/β/γ, cyclin D1)",
    "Marker group assigned →\nadaptive randomization engine"))
ba <- data.frame(x = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6), xend = c(4.6, 4.6, 4.6, 4.6),
                 y = c(8.58, 6.73, 4.88, 2.83), yend = c(8.38, 6.53, 4.68, 2.63))
flow_diagram(bx, ba, ylim = c(0.6, 10)) +
  annotate("text", x = 9.15, y = c(9.2, 7.35, 5.5, 3.65, 1.7), size = 2.6,
           colour = "grey35", hjust = 0.5,
           label = c("day 0", "day 0", "≤ day 1", "≤ 2 weeks", "≤ 2 weeks")) +
  labs(title = "From needle to randomization in about two weeks")

```

The pipeline had a second, forward-looking layer: alongside the clinical-trial cores, **additional tissue (and blood/serum) was banked for discovery** — the raw material for later BATTLE-derived papers on KRAS variant biology, an EMT resistance signature, and sorafenib sensitivity signatures (Section 7.4) [@kim2011; @liu2015].


# Implementation and operations: where adaptive designs actually live
<br>
## The information system
<br>
BATTLE treated the adaptive design as a real-time information system. An integrated web application tracked patients from registration and biopsy through biomarker classification, randomization, 8-week assessment, and follow-up. Data were stored in MD Anderson's CORe environment and a study-specific SQL Server database [@liu2015]. R code, invoked through web services, automatically updated posterior DCRs, randomization probabilities, and futility decisions whenever an outcome was recorded [@liu2015]. This infrastructure illustrates the practical costs of adaptive trials: timely data entry, quality control, computation, and specialized software [@leechu2012].
<br>
Endpoint timeliness was critical. Automated reminders prompted coordinators to schedule week-8 scans and escalated outcomes overdue by more than two weeks [@liu2015]. A multidisciplinary endpoint committee, blinded to treatment assignment, adjudicated RECIST outcomes before they entered the randomization algorithm [@liu2015].
<br>
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Why blinded adjudication mattered
Each 8-week outcome influenced allocations for future patients. Knowledge of treatment could bias assessments, particularly stable-disease classifications, and propagate that bias through the adaptive algorithm. Blinded adjudication is therefore an important safeguard in outcome-adaptive trials [@liu2015].
:::
<br>
## Implementation lessons
<br>
BATTLE required close coordination among clinicians, radiologists, pathologists, pharmacists, nurses, programmers, coordinators, and statisticians [@liu2015]. Its retrospective evaluation identified five main lessons [@liu2015; @kim2011]:

1. **Marker grouping diluted signals.** Combining *EGFR* mutations with copy-number changes weakened predictive performance, while several prespecified markers were uninformative. Marker groupings should remain flexible when prior evidence is limited.
2. **Burn-in delayed adaptation.** Requiring observations in every cell postponed adaptive randomization until approximately 40% of patients had enrolled. The investigators later recommended adapting after about 20–25%.
3. **Eligibility restricted adaptation.** Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four treatments, so most allocations occurred within restricted arm sets $\Omega$ (@eq-ar).
4. **Population drift changed eligibility.** Increasing proportions of smokers and patients previously treated with erlotinib altered the available treatment sets. Adaptive trials should monitor such drift and consider covariate adjustment.
5. **Adaptation depends on biological separation.** Outcome-adaptive randomization offers limited gains when treatments or biomarkers do not meaningfully discriminate outcomes [@liu2015; @lee2012adapt].
<br>
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## BATTLE-2: redesigning around the lessons
BATTLE-2 introduced adaptive randomization from the first patient, bounded allocation probabilities, and no prespecified marker groups. Candidate biomarkers were screened before the trial and evaluated through a Bayesian two-stage Lasso strategy. The design also added a stage-1 Go/No-Go decision, futility monitoring from patient 71, and a target of 400 evaluable patients, with at least 80% power and a 10% type I error rate. Following a January 2013 FDA meeting, the trial received an investigational device exemption waiver [@liu2015; @lee2010; @gu2013lasso; @gu2014].
:::

# Documented results: what 244 evaluable patients showed

## Patient flow and exposure

@fig-consort lays out the documented flow. One quarter of enrolled patients (86 of 341) never reached randomization — the price of a biopsy-mandated design in a rapidly declining population — and the arm-level counts already hint at the adaptation to come.

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "BATTLE-1 patient flow (documented counts from the CONSORT diagram of @kim2011). Of 341 enrolled patients (Nov 2006 – Oct 2009), 255 were randomized — 97 by equal randomization and 158 adaptively — and 244 had an evaluable 8-week disease-control status. The 86 never randomized: 51 for concurrent illness or deteriorating performance status, 17 for conditions preventing biopsy, and 18 who chose alternative treatment. Seventeen patients were randomized twice and one three times (re-entry after progression with a new biopsy)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.6
cx <- data.frame(
  x = c(1.55, 5.0, 8.45, 5.0),
  y = c(7.6, 7.6, 7.6, 3.4),

           label = "Randomized per arm: erlotinib 59 • vandetanib 54 • erlotinib + bexarotene 37 • sorafenib 105\nEvaluable for 8-week DCR per arm: 58 • 52 • 36 • 98 (Table 2 of Kim et al. 2011)") +

```

The randomized population was characteristically hard: median age 62 (range 26–84), 54% male, 63% adenocarcinoma, 69% former smokers, ECOG 0–1 in 85%, median two prior chemotherapy regimens, 45% previously treated with erlotinib, and 33% with prior brain metastases. Mutation prevalence: *EGFR* 15%, *KRAS* 20% [@kim2011].

## Overall efficacy, and the primary endpoint

Among the **244** patients evaluable at 8 weeks, the overall DCR@8w was **46%** (112/244), with **no complete responses and only 9 partial responses** — typical cytostatic activity for targeted agents in this setting. Median PFS was **1.9 months** (95% CI 1.8–2.4), median OS **8.8 months** (95% CI 6.4–10.6), and 1-year survival **35%**. In a pre-specified-style landmark analysis anchored at week 8, patients with disease control lived longer (median 9.6 months, 95% CI 7.4–12.5) than those without (7.5 months, 95% CI 4.2–9.2; P = 0.018) [@kim2011]. Treatment-related grade 3–4 toxicity was **6.5%** and compliance exceeded 95% in every arm; sorafenib caused the most toxicity (treatment discontinuation in 19%, dose reductions in 21%) [@kim2011].

To visualize the marginal results with honest uncertainty, we recompute **Wilson score intervals** (@eq-wilson) from the documented counts and plot them in @fig-dcr-arms — a reconstruction of published summaries, not new inference on patient-level data:

$$
\tilde p = \frac{\hat p + z^2/(2n)}{1 + z^2/n}, \qquad
\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\gamma) =
\tilde p \pm \frac{z}{1 + z^2/n}\,
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p (1 - \hat p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4 n^2}}
$$ {#eq-wilson}

In @eq-wilson, $\hat p = x/n$ is the observed DCR in a cell with $x$ disease-control successes among $n$ evaluable patients and $z = 1.96$ for a 95% interval; $\tilde p$ is the interval's center, pulled slightly toward 1/2 relative to $\hat p$. The Wilson interval behaves well for the small cell counts ($n$ as low as 3) that adaptive trials inevitably produce — unlike the Wald interval, it never leaves $[0,1]$ and stays sane near the boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dcr-arms
#| fig-cap: "Documented 8-week disease control by arm, with 95% Wilson intervals (@eq-wilson) computed from the published counts — erlotinib 20/58, vandetanib 17/52, erlotinib + bexarotene 18/36, sorafenib 57/98 [@kim2011]; the sorafenib interval brackets the 58.2% reported by the arm's final paper [@blumenschein2013]. Dashed line: 30% historical DCR benchmark used in the success rule [@kim2011; @lara2008]. This is a marginal, all-comers view — the design's inference lives at the arm × marker-group level (Fig. @fig-heatmap)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
wilson <- function(x, n, z = 1.959964) {
  p <- x / n
  d <- 1 + z^2 / n
  ctr <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / d
  hw  <- (z / d) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))
  c(ctr - hw, ctr + hw)
}
arms_df <- data.frame(
  arm = c("Erlotinib", "Vandetanib", "Erlotinib +\nbexarotene", "Sorafenib"),
  x = c(20, 17, 18, 57),
  n = c(58, 52, 36, 98))
ci_ar <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(arms_df)), function(i) wilson(arms_df$x[i], arms_df$n[i])))
arms_df$pct <- 100 * arms_df$x / arms_df$n
arms_df$lo  <- 100 * ci_ar[, 1]
arms_df$hi  <- 100 * ci_ar[, 2]
ggplot(arms_df, aes(arm, pct, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.62, colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.09, linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 30, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(x, "/", n, "  (", round(pct), "%)")),
            vjust = -1.0, size = 3.0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal[1:4]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 85), labels = percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "8-week disease control rate",
       title = "Marginal DCR@8w by arm (documented counts, Wilson 95% CIs)") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.62, y = 31.5, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           hjust = 0, label = "historical 30% DCR benchmark")

```

## The heart of BATTLE: the arm × marker-group matrix

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dcr
#| tbl-cap: "Documented 8-week disease control by treatment and marker group (Table 2 of @kim2011). Cells marked * were declared 'effective' per the design's success rule, Pr(DCR > 30% | data) ≥ 0.80. Note the emptiness of the RXR/cyclin D1 row (only six patients) — the sparse cell that delayed adaptive randomization and later motivated the no-grouping redesign of BATTLE-2 [@liu2015]."
#| echo: true
dcr_cells <- tribble(
  ~group, ~erlotinib, ~vandetanib, ~elo_bex, ~sorafenib,
  "EGFR",           "6/17 (35%)",  "11/27 (41%)*", "11/20 (55%)*", "9/23 (39%)",
  "KRAS/BRAF",      "1/7 (14%)",   "0/3 (0%)",     "1/3 (33%)",    "11/14 (79%)*",
  "VEGF/VEGFR-2",   "10/25 (40%)*","6/16 (38%)",   "0/3 (0%)",     "25/39 (64%)*",
  "RXR/cyclin D1",  "0/1 (0%)",    "—",            "1/1 (100%)*",  "1/4 (25%)",
  "None/unknown",   "3/8 (38%)",   "0/6 (0%)",     "5/9 (56%)*",   "11/18 (61%)*",
  "Total",          "20/58 (34%)", "17/52 (33%)",  "18/36 (50%)",  "57/98 (58%)"
)
colnames(dcr_cells) <- c("Marker group", "Erlotinib", "Vandetanib",
                         "Erlotinib + bexarotene", "Sorafenib")
knitr::kable(dcr_cells, align = "lrrrr")

```

Read @tbl-dcr — visualized as a heatmap in @fig-heatmap — the way the design intended: *down columns* are conventional marginal results; *across rows* is the trial's real hypothesis test — within a marker group, which targeted agent controls disease? Sorafenib's 79% (11/14) in *KRAS/BRAF*-mutant tumors against 14% for erlotinib and 0% for vandetanib is the pattern a biomarker-guided trial exists to find, and it confirmed the prespecified hypothesis for sorafenib in that class [@kim2011].

```{r}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "The same documented matrix as a heatmap (percentages; '—' marks a cell with no patients). Asterisks denote the design's 'effective' declarations — posterior probability of exceeding the 30% benchmark of at least 0.80 [@kim2011]. Effective pairings: erlotinib in VEGF/VEGFR-2; vandetanib in EGFR; erlotinib + bexarotene in EGFR, RXR/cyclin D1 and none/unknown; sorafenib in KRAS/BRAF, VEGF/VEGFR-2 and none/unknown. The RXR/cyclin D1 row shows what tiny cell sizes do to a posterior — one success out of one patient yields a strikingly high posterior mean under a vague prior, a useful teaching point about hierarchical models with vague hyperpriors."
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
hm <- tribble(
  ~group, ~arm, ~x, ~n, ~eff,
  "EGFR",          "Erlotinib",  6, 17, FALSE,
  "EGFR",          "Vandetanib", 11, 27, TRUE,
  "EGFR",          "E+B",        11, 20, TRUE,
  "EGFR",          "Sorafenib",  9, 23, FALSE,
  "KRAS/BRAF",     "Erlotinib",  1, 7, FALSE,
  "KRAS/BRAF",     "Vandetanib", 0, 3, FALSE,
  "KRAS/BRAF",     "E+B",        1, 3, FALSE,
  "KRAS/BRAF",     "Sorafenib",  11, 14, TRUE,
  "VEGF/VEGFR-2",  "Erlotinib",  10, 25, TRUE,
  "VEGF/VEGFR-2",  "Vandetanib", 6, 16, FALSE,
  "VEGF/VEGFR-2",  "E+B",        0, 3, FALSE,
  "VEGF/VEGFR-2",  "Sorafenib",  25, 39, TRUE,
  "RXR/cyclin D1", "Erlotinib",  0, 1, FALSE,
  "RXR/cyclin D1", "Vandetanib", 0, 0, FALSE,
  "RXR/cyclin D1", "E+B",        1, 1, TRUE,
  "RXR/cyclin D1", "Sorafenib",  1, 4, FALSE,
  "None/unknown",  "Erlotinib",  3, 8, FALSE,
  "None/unknown",  "Vandetanib", 0, 6, FALSE,
  "None/unknown",  "E+B",        5, 9, TRUE,
  "None/unknown",  "Sorafenib",  11, 18, TRUE)
hm$pct <- ifelse(hm$n == 0, NA_real_, 100 * hm$x / hm$n)
hm$lab <- ifelse(hm$n == 0, "—",
                 paste0(hm$x, "/", hm$n, "  (", round(hm$pct), "%)",
                        ifelse(hm$eff, " *", "")))
ggplot(hm, aes(factor(arm, levels = c("Erlotinib", "Vandetanib", "E+B", "Sorafenib")),
               factor(group, levels = rev(c("EGFR", "KRAS/BRAF",
        "VEGF/VEGFR-2", "RXR/cyclin D1", "None/unknown"))), fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), size = 3.05, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F4FAFF", high = pal[1], na.value = "grey92") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "DCR@8w",
       title = "Documented DCR@8w: treatment × marker-group matrix") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

## Did adaptation actually happen? Yes — visibly

Equal randomization would have put ~64 patients per arm; @fig-allocation plots the divergence. The documented final allocation — 105 to sorafenib versus 58 erlotinib, 52 vandetanib, 36 erlotinib + bexarotene — is the adaptive engine made visible: as evidence accumulated, the marginal DCR leader received increasingly more patients [@kim2011; @liu2015].

```{r}
#| label: fig-allocation
#| fig-cap: "Documented final allocation vs. equal randomization. Bars: patients randomized per arm (n = 255 randomized assignments; 17 patients contributed two assignments and one three, per @kim2011); the dashed line marks equal allocation (255/4 ≈ 64). Marginal DCRs (34/33/50/58%) are annotated. The allocational skew tracks the observed marginal DCRs — the qualitative signature of outcome-adaptive randomization [@kim2011; @liu2015]."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
al <- data.frame(
  arm = c("Erlotinib", "Vandetanib", "Erlotinib +\nbexarotene", "Sorafenib"),
  n_rand = c(59, 54, 37, 105),
  dcr = c(34, 33, 50, 58))
ggplot(al, aes(arm, n_rand, fill = arm)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.62, colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 255 / 4, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n_rand, "  (DCR ", dcr, "%)")),
            vjust = -0.9, size = 3.0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal[1:4]) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 130)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Patients randomized",
       title = "Final allocation: the adaptive engine's fingerprint") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.62, y = 67, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35", hjust = 0,
           label = "equal allocation (≈64/arm)")

```

## The individual-marker story the grouping obscured

The team's prespecified and exploratory single-marker analyses — run *after* the marker-group model had done its allocation work — sharpen the picture [@kim2011; @liu2015]:

- *EGFR* mutation predicted better 8-week control on **erlotinib** (P = 0.04): 71% DCR in *EGFR*-mutant versus 29% in wild-type tumors [@liu2015].
- High **VEGFR-2** expression predicted benefit from **vandetanib** (P = 0.05), consistent with the arm's mechanism [@kim2011].
- High **cyclin D1** expression (P = 0.01) and *EGFR* amplification (P = 0.006) predicted benefit from **erlotinib + bexarotene** — the RXR/cyclin D1 hypothesis finally visible only at the individual-marker level [@kim2011].
- For **sorafenib**, DCR was 64% in *EGFR*-wild-type tumors versus 33% for all other treatments combined (P < 0.001), with a trend in *KRAS*-mutant tumors (61% vs 32%, P = 0.11) [@kim2011]; *EGFR* mutation (P = 0.01) and high polysomy (P = 0.05) predicted *worse* control on sorafenib [@kim2011].

@fig-markers draws these contrasts side by side.

```{r}
#| label: fig-markers
#| fig-cap: "Documented single-marker contrasts of 8-week DCR (percentages as published; p-values from the primary paper). Each row compares a treatment's performance across marker-defined strata of the same patients. Sources: 71% vs 29% and 61% vs 22% from @liu2015; 64% vs 33% (P < 0.001) and 61% vs 32% (P = 0.11) from @kim2011. The top row is why the trialists later regretted bundling EGFR mutation with copy-number markers: the grouped analysis understated the strongest signal in the trial."
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
mk <- data.frame(
  contrast = c("EGFR-mutant vs EGFR-wild-type\n(on erlotinib)",
               "KRAS-mutant: sorafenib vs erlotinib",
               "EGFR-wild-type: sorafenib vs\nall other arms",
               "KRAS-mutant: sorafenib vs\nall other arms"),
  lo = c(29, 22, 33, 32),
  hi = c(71, 61, 64, 61),
  p  = c("P = 0.04", "P not reported", "P < 0.001", "P = 0.11"))
mk$contrast <- factor(mk$contrast, levels = rev(mk$contrast))
ggplot(mk, aes(x = lo, xend = hi, y = contrast, yend = contrast)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 30, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 1.6, colour = "grey55",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.14, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = lo), size = 3.4, colour = pal[2]) +
  geom_point(aes(x = hi), size = 3.4, colour = pal[1]) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = contrast, label = p),
            vjust = -1.05, size = 2.85, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(15, 80)) +
  labs(x = "8-week disease control rate", y = NULL,
       title = "Single-marker contrasts (orange = comparator, blue = experimental)")

```

## Arm postscripts published after the main paper

Three of the four arms received dedicated final publications that deepen the results in instructive ways. The **sorafenib** analysis confirmed the marginal DCR of 58.2% (98 evaluable), median PFS 2.83 months (95% CI 2.04–3.58) and OS 8.48 months (95% CI 5.78–10.97); DCR was higher in *EGFR*-wild-type than *EGFR*-mutant tumors (P = 0.012), and a gene-expression "sorafenib sensitivity signature" built from cell lines and BATTLE biopsies separated PFS (3.61 vs 1.84 months, P = 0.026) [@blumenschein2013]. The **vandetanib** report showed overall activity (DCR 33%, median PFS 1.81 months, median OS 6.5 months) with an exploratory hint of benefit from dual VEGFR/EGFR blockade in *EGFR*-mutant, TKI-resistant tumors but no overall survival advantage [@tsao2013]. An **elderly-subgroup** analysis found signals such as better PFS with vandetanib in men aged 65–70 and with sorafenib in men over 70 [@tsao2012]. Banked specimens additionally yielded the KRAS-variant biology analysis [@ihle2012] and the 76-gene EMT resistance signature [@byers2013].

```{r}
#| label: fig-survival
#| fig-cap: "Illustrative reconstruction — exponential survival curves calibrated to the published median PFS (1.9 months) and OS (8.8 months) for the overall randomized population [@kim2011]. Under an exponential model with median m, S(t) = 0.5^(t/m) (@eq-exp). These are NOT Kaplan–Meier estimates from patient-level data — real curves bend and cross subgroups differently — but they give an honest visual sense of the temporal scale on which the 8-week endpoint sits: by the time the median patient had died, nearly a year had passed; by week 8 (dashed), most patients were still progression-free."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.8
tt <- seq(0, 24, by = 0.05)
surv_df <- data.frame(
  t = rep(tt, 2),
  S = c(0.5^(tt / 1.9), 0.5^(tt / 8.8)),
  curve = rep(c("PFS (median 1.9 months)", "OS (median 8.8 months)"),
              each = length(tt)))
ggplot(surv_df, aes(t, 100 * S, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = 3, colour = "grey60") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[1], pal[4])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomization", y = "Event-free proportion",
       title = "Illustrative exponential reconstruction of the published medians") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 93, size = 2.9, colour = "grey35",
           label = "week 8: the primary endpoint's clock")

```

$$
S(t) = 0.5^{\,t / m}
$$ {#eq-exp}

In @eq-exp, $S(t)$ is the event-free proportion at time $t$ and $m$ the median event time in months; the exponential is the unique survival model in which the hazard is constant, and it is used here purely as a visual calibration device, not as an inferential claim.


# Regulatory interactions, guidance, and the path to acceptance

Because adaptive and biomarker-guided designs live or die by regulatory acceptance, this section addresses the question directly and in two layers: what is *documented* about BATTLE's own regulatory interactions, and how the *surrounding regulatory framework* evolved around trials like it. Where we move from record to interpretation, we say so.

## What is actually documented about BATTLE and regulators

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Fact box — documented regulatory touchpoints of the BATTLE program
- **Oversight of BATTLE-1** was conventional and documented: approval by the MD Anderson IRB and the U.S. Department of Defense, monitoring by an independent DSMB (chaired by Donald A. Berry), and standard IND-era handling of the investigational agents [@kim2011].
- **Agent status mattered.** Two of the four agents were FDA-approved at the time (erlotinib, Nov 2004 [@cohen2005]; sorafenib, Dec 2005, for renal-cell carcinoma [@kane2006]); vandetanib was not approved anywhere until April 2011 [@vandetanib2011]; the erlotinib + bexarotene combination was investigational [@kim2011]. BATTLE-1 was thus an investigator-initiated phase II platform, not a registration program.
- **The documented FDA interaction belongs to BATTLE-2**: "Due to its exploratory nature, BATTLE-2 has received the investigational device exemption (IDE) waiver after a meeting with the FDA in January 2013" [@liu2015]. The trial's biopsy-and-biomarker workflow is what brings it into IDE territory, and the sponsor sought and documented FDA input on the adaptive design before opening stage 1 (trial registration NCT01248247; opened June 2011 at MD Anderson and Yale).
- **Industry engaged publicly**: the primary BATTLE-1 paper drew a companion commentary from scientists at Merck Research Laboratories framing the trial as "a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development" and highlighting simultaneous therapeutics–diagnostics development [@rubin2011]; Merck scientists (D. Mauro, E. Rubin) later co-authored the BATTLE-2 primary paper [@papadim2016].
- To our knowledge, **no public record documents a special FDA review of BATTLE-1's adaptive features** of the kind later formalized in FDA's adaptive-design guidance processes — consistent with its role as an exploratory, single-center, non-registration platform. (This is a statement about the absence of public documentation, not about private interactions.)
:::

## Interpretation: what BATTLE did and did not change for regulators

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Interpretation (clearly not a documented causal claim)
BATTLE was never a registration trial, and it left no documented regulatory decision trail of its own. Its regulatory significance is better understood as **feasibility testimony and methodological exemplar**: it demonstrated to sponsors and reviewers alike that biopsy-mandated, biomarker-stratified, adaptively randomized platforms can be executed and monitored, and its statistical grammar — hierarchical models, posterior decision thresholds, simulated operating characteristics, prespecified adaptation rules — is precisely the grammar the 2019 FDA guidance later asks sponsors to speak [@fda2019; @liu2015; @leechu2012]. Three specific contrasts between BATTLE-style exploration and registration expectations are worth teaching:

1. **Error budgets.** A deliberate 20% per-cell type I error rate is defensible for discovery platforms; regulators evaluating confirmatory claims ask for controlled family-wise (or at least clearly bounded) error across the adaptation and subgroup structure — the EMA paper and FDA final guidance both make this central [@ema2007; @fda2019].
2. **Endpoint.** An 8-week DCR enabled the adaptation but would not, by itself, support a therapeutic claim; registration examples of biomarker-guided approval (e.g., the erlotinib–cobas EGFR co-approval) rested on survival-benefit endpoints with validated diagnostics [@fdacdx2013; @cohen2005].
3. **Device–drug coupling.** BATTLE used biomarkers for *allocation learning*, not for *device-regulated patient selection claims*; the regulatory machinery for the latter (co-development, CDx PMA) is what later made biomarker-guided labels routine [@fdacodev2014; @fdaenrich2019].

In our reading, BATTLE's most durable regulatory contribution is cultural: along with I-SPY 2 [@barker2009], it normalized the idea that a trial's *decision engine* can learn while protecting patients — and the eventual ICH E20 draft is, in effect, the codification of lessons from this generation of platform trials [@iche20; @berry2012].
:::

# Legacy: BATTLE-2 and the platform-trial era

## BATTLE-2: the redesign, honestly reported

BATTLE-2 (NCT01248247) redesigned the platform around every lesson of BATTLE-1: adaptive randomization **from the first patient**, stratified by *KRAS* status with probabilities bounded at 0.2–0.8 (stage 1) and 0.1–0.9 (stage 2); no prespecified marker grouping (>100 candidate markers screened pre-trial, refined in-trial via training–testing–validation and a Bayesian two-step Lasso); a Go/No-Go gate after stage 1; futility monitoring from patient 71; 450 planned enrollments (400 evaluable); and a documented FDA meeting (January 2013) with IDE waiver [@liu2015; @lee2010; @gu2014; @gu2013lasso]. The design and other feature of the trial will be discussed in other article.


## The era BATTLE helped open

Contemporaneous commentaries recognized the moment — "a new BATTLE in the evolving war on cancer" [@sequist2011], and, from Merck, "a bold step toward improving the efficiency of biomarker-based drug development" [@rubin2011]. The direct descendants are familiar. **I-SPY 2** embedded biomarker-adaptive randomization with Bayesian "graduation" rules in breast cancer [@barker2009]. **NCI-MATCH** and **Lung-MAP** made molecular screening plus biomarker-matched assignment national infrastructure [@ncimatch; @lungmap]. Reviewers of adaptive oncology cite BATTLE as the completed proof-of-concept for Bayesian adaptive, biomarker-guided randomization [@berry2012; @leechu2012; @liu2015]. And the specific design ideas — hierarchical borrowing across subgroups, posterior-probability decision rules, allocation floors and bounds, burn-in stages — are now standard vocabulary in trial-design software and ICH E20 discussions [@iche20; @berrybook2010].

# Ten lessons for designing and analyzing biomarker-guided adaptive trials

1. **Operations are the design.** The binding constraint on BATTLE was never computation; it was biopsy adequacy (82.9%), assay turnaround (2 weeks), and endpoint timeliness. Before promising any adaptation, measure — and prespecify minimum acceptable values for — the operational chain that feeds it [@tam2013; @liu2015].
2. **Pick an endpoint that outruns accrual.** Adaptive randomization only helps if outcomes arrive faster than patients. The 8-week DCR was chosen for exactly this property and had survival-prediction evidence behind it [@lara2008; @zhou2008].
3. **Budget the burn-in, don't let it happen to you.** Equal randomization builds the prior, but a "wait until every cell is filled" rule handed the calendar to the sparsest subgroup (~40% of the trial ran equally). A fixed proportion (20–25%) or model-based readiness criteria are safer [@liu2015].
4. **Don't bundle biomarkers you mean to learn about.** Grouping preserved degrees of freedom but diluted *EGFR*-mutation signal and wasted the trial's sparsest groups on uninformative RXR markers. Group only when prior evidence is genuinely symmetric across constituents; otherwise model individual markers [@kim2011; @liu2015].
5. **Keep allocation floors/bounds — and justify them by simulation.** The 10% floor kept every open arm learnable; BATTLE-2's 0.2–0.8 and 0.1–0.9 bounds prevent both starvation and premature commitment. Show that operating characteristics survive perturbing these constants (@fig-sensitivity) [@zhou2008; @liu2015].
6. **Simulate the eligibility structure, not just the biology.** Only 14% of patients were eligible for all four arms; the effective randomization space is the intersection of futility, eligibility, and marker group. Your simulations should mimic that intersection [@liu2015].
7. **State decision thresholds and their error trade-off in advance.** Null 30% / target 50% / success at 80% posterior / futility at 10% posterior — all prespecified, all calibrated by simulation, with the 20% type I error rate defended openly as a screening choice [@zhou2008; @kim2011].
8. **Make futility reversible and adjudicate endpoints blinded.** Cell-level suspension that can reopen, plus an endpoint review committee blinded to assignment, protects the integrity of the feedback loop into randomization [@zhou2008; @liu2015].
9. **Watch for drift and say what adaptation does to comparisons.** Monitor enrollment mix prospectively (BATTLE's smokers/prior-erlotinib drift); plan covariate adjustment for between-arm contrasts, because adaptive allocation entangles arm with calendar time [@liu2015].
10. **Separate the engine from the verdict.** BATTLE's adaptive machinery learned which cells were promising; it did not — and was never designed to — establish comparative efficacy. Design the confirmation path (randomized comparison, validated diagnostic, appropriate error budget) as part of the platform, not afterthought [@kim2011; @ema2007; @fda2019].
